intro: You asked for outreach to companies that fit the MTP. I screened all 20 contributors in SpaceCom Second Stage's 'LEO and Beyond: In-Space Infrastructure' spotlight (spacecomsecondstage.com) against 'Make Every Space Vehicle Reusable' and checked each one against the live CRM. Tier 1 (drafts 1-7) are IPS / reusability partner plays: they build vehicles that need lighter, refillable, cryo-capable pressurized structures. Tier 2 (drafts 8-11) are 'prove the systems before risking the orbital vehicle' flight-test plays. Each draft is in your ready-to-send format: recipient on the first line, then the subject, then the letter. Your Outlook signature adds the company block. Blanks marked [____] are yours to fill. Per your standing rule there will be no follow-up nags from me. Where a warm intro path exists I've noted it, and I'd use that path over a cold send.
excluded: Palantir (Sammy Moseley), Amentum, HawkEye 360 (Patrick Zeitouni): software, ground and RF-ISR. They don't build vehicles, so there's no IPS or reuse hook.
The Aerospace Corporation (Bryan Hoke): FFRDC/government. Any approach goes through you, not cold BD.
ISS National Lab, Lt. Gen. John Shaw (ret.): institutional and thought-leadership contributors. Shaw is a possible advisor or conference contact, not a customer.
BioOrbit (Katie King) and Star Catcher (Andrew Rush): both got payload pitches in Jul/Aug 2026 (tasks #1446, #1873) with no reply logged. Skipped under the no-nag rule.
Cosmic Shielding: suborbital flight gives very little radiation dose, so we have no honest test value to offer them.
claims: MTP and IPS wording come from the canonical one-pager and narrative (drafts/Exos_MTP_OnePager_Make_Every_Space_Vehicle_Reusable_2026-09-20.md; mc /mtp.html).

Scorpius Type V tanks flew on Intuitive Machines IM-2 (Athena): https://www.compositesworld.com/news/scorpius-type-5-tanks-underpin-second-intuitive-machines-mission-to-the-moon and https://scorpius.com/scorpius-space-launch-companys-methane-and-liquid-oxygen-tanks-fueling-intuitive-machines-im-2-athena-lunar-lander-on-its-journey-to-the-moon

Exos has flown commercial payloads since 2018 (SARGE), and BLK3 is our latest FAA-licensed vehicle, licensed 3/13/26. BLK3 timing is stated only as 'early 2027'. No pricing, no 'one of only three' claim, no RDRE or propulsion-provider language.
Each recipient's program is paraphrased from their own SpaceCom Second Stage article (Oct 2026), linked in each note.

drafts.subject: Your “Unpredictable Advantage” piece, and refillable tankage for Ranger
drafts.body:
Jim,

I read your SpaceCom Second Stage piece on mobility and refueling as the infrastructure of competitive endurance. It lines up almost exactly with where Exos has planted its flag. Our purpose is to make every space vehicle reusable, and the hard part of that isn't recovery. It's building structures and propellant systems that survive repeated cryogenic cycling, long-duration storage and refueling.

That's our Integrated Pressurized Structures (IPS) platform: Type V composite pressure vessels built into the load-bearing structure, from the same tank family our affiliate Scorpius flew to the Moon on Intuitive Machines' IM-2 lander. We are pairing it with zero-loss cryogenic transfer work with Princeton Cryogenics.

For a maneuverable vehicle like Ranger, lighter and refillable tankage turns into more maneuver per mission and a vehicle that can be topped off instead of replaced. I'd like to put our IPS team in front of Steven and your engineers for an hour to see where it fits on your roadmap.

Separately, thank you again for the Claremore introduction. [____ one line on where Claremore stands ____]

Best,
John

drafts.subject: Pre-positioned carriers + Viper: lighter pressurized structure and refillable propellant
drafts.body:
Colin,

Your SpaceCom Second Stage piece on pre-positioned orbital carriers made a strong case: stage the capability in orbit, then move it when it's needed. That architecture only pays off if the carriers and the vehicles that leave them can be refilled and reused many times.

That is the problem Exos is built around. Our purpose is to make every space vehicle reusable, and our enabling technology is Integrated Pressurized Structures (IPS): Type V composite pressure vessels that serve as load-bearing structure and hold up to repeated cryogenic cycling. It's the same tank family our affiliate Scorpius flew to the Moon on Intuitive Machines' IM-2. We're pairing it with zero-loss cryogenic transfer work with Princeton Cryogenics.

Two places I think we can help Gravitics. First, propellant storage and transfer hardware for the carriers as refueling nodes and for Viper OTX. Second, flight validation on BLK3, our reusable FAA-licensed suborbital vehicle, so subsystems see real launch loads and come back for inspection before they're committed to orbit.

Would you be open to a 30-minute call with our engineering lead to see whether either is worth pursuing?

Best,
John

drafts.subject: The reusable satellite, and the structure that has to survive the return
drafts.body:
Brian,

I enjoyed your SpaceCom Second Stage piece on the reusable satellite: return, refurbish, upgrade and relaunch. Exos's stated purpose is to make every space vehicle reusable, so we are about as aligned as two companies can be.

I wrote in August about flight-testing re-entry hardware. The bigger opportunity is the structure. Repeated return-and-relaunch cycles are hard on pressure vessels and propellant systems. Our Integrated Pressurized Structures (IPS) platform uses Type V composite vessels built as load-bearing structure and qualified for repeated cryogenic cycling. It's the same tank family our affiliate Scorpius flew to the Moon on Intuitive Machines' IM-2, and it's designed to be refilled rather than thrown away.

If it's useful, our reusable suborbital vehicle can also fly Delphi subsystems through real launch and descent loads and hand them back for inspection before you commit them to orbit.

Worth 30 minutes to compare notes on where the structure and propulsion stack is heading?

Best,
John

Your SpaceCom Second Stage piece reframed propellant from a finite spacecraft resource into orbital infrastructure. I think that's exactly right, and it puts a new requirement on hardware: tanks and transfer systems that can be cycled, refilled and stored for years without degrading.

That is what Exos builds toward. Our purpose is to make every space vehicle reusable, and our enabling technology is Integrated Pressurized Structures (IPS): lightweight Type V composite pressure vessels built for repeated cryogenic loading and long-duration storage. drafts.subject: Maneuver without regret starts with the tank
drafts.body:
Kara,

Your SpaceCom Second Stage piece on maneuvering without regret framed the real constraint well. Operators ration every maneuver because propellant and the hardware that holds it are finite.

Exos works on the other half of that equation. Our purpose is to make every space vehicle reusable, and our enabling technology is Integrated Pressurized Structures (IPS): Type V composite pressure vessels built into load-bearing structure, lighter than conventional tankage and built for repeated cryogenic cycling and refueling. It's the same tank family our affiliate Scorpius flew to the Moon on Intuitive Machines' IM-2.

Paired with Agile's thrusters, lighter and refillable tankage means more delta-v per kilogram and spacecraft that can be topped off instead of retired. Our reusable FAA-licensed suborbital vehicle can also host propulsion and subsystem experiments, with approval, under real flight loads before they go to orbit.

Would a 30-minute intro call with our engineering team make sense?

Best,
John

drafts.subject: Extend, clear, repeat, and fly it before you fly it
drafts.body:
Michael,

Your SpaceCom Second Stage piece on servicing as a way to extend life and clear orbit is the reuse mindset applied to the whole orbital economy. That's very close to Exos's purpose: make every space vehicle reusable.

We can help in two ways. First, Exos operates BLK3, our latest FAA-licensed reusable suborbital vehicle (Exos has flown commercial payloads since 2018). Servicing teams can fly sensors, GNC components and capture mechanisms through real launch, vacuum and descent loads and get the hardware back within days, before risking an Otter on orbit. Second, our Integrated Pressurized Structures (IPS) platform provides lightweight, refillable Type V composite tankage. It's the same family our affiliate Scorpius flew to the Moon on Intuitive Machines' IM-2, which matters for a servicer that should itself be refuelable.

Open to a short call to see whether either fits your next build?

Best,
John
